title: Cops are using AI to spy on you
content:
American police departments are using secretive AI technology to create lifelike AI personas designed to interact with real people online —like protesters and activists— for intelligence gathering.

This tech is becoming more popular amid crackdowns on student protests against the killing in Gaza. Leaked presentations reveal AI personas posing as various people, from divorced moms to teenage boys, in attempts to infiltrate online communities.

404 Media's Jason Koebler joined me on this week’s Power User podcast to break down how these police-created AI personas work, how they're being deployed, how to identify them, and what role AI plays in the future of surveillance. Subscribe to my YouTube channel for more!

All those ‘deinfluencing’ trend pieces were lying to you

Every couple of years, there’s an endless barrage of headlines about how the creator economy has peaked. These headlines and videos rack up millions of views. But a new report published by the Interactive Advertising Bureau, shows just false they are. The creator industry is very much not dying, according to the numbers, it's thriving and growing exponentially.

The number of full-time content creators in the U.S. skyrocketed from 200,000 in 2020 to 1.5 million full-time content creators in 2024— a 7.5x jump in just four years. While headlines bemoan the supposed death of influencing and the "creator bubble," the sector has become the fastest-growing segment of online jobs.

While “deinfluencing” might seem like a grassroots revolt against content creators, it has been grossly mischaracterized by legacy news outlets desperate for a convenient narrative. Deinfluencing isn’t about ending creator culture. It’s about creators centering trust and transparency instead of doing low quality sponcon.

Creator media revenue is now growing five times faster than the traditional media sector, the IAB report found. In 2008, the internet contributed just 2% of the U.S. GDP. Today, it supports $4.9 trillion (18% of the economy) and it’s the leading driver of GDP growth. Creator jobs now comprise 30% of all digital economy employment, while gig economy platforms like Uber, DoorDash, and Airbnb account for just 8%.

Niche Los Angeles coffee shop drama

This has been all over TikTok, but as a Los Angeles resident I need to fill you in on something that is tearing our city apart. Maru coffee, a hot spot, extremely pretentious coffee shop in L.A. became famous for their "cream top" coffee, which is just an iced Americano with sweetened condensed cream as a big thick layer on top. People became so obsessed with the cream top that Maru started selling it on the side.

Naturally, people started putting the cream top on all sorts of different beverages, especially their matcha. Now, Maru coffee is refusing to sell the cream tops on the side anymore because they want to ensure that each beverage is “well balanced” and basically they’re grossed out by people putting the cream top on other, “non approved” beverages. This has led to a meltdown and basically a boycott of Maru coffee until they bring back the cream top.
